Few-shot chain-of-thought is an in-context learning technique; if emergent abilities are in-context learning, the chain-of-thought threshold is the in-context-learning threshold. Wang's finding that invalid demonstrations still work points the same way.

Both concern GSM8K staying at floor until a threshold; Du et al. place it in pre-training loss rather than parameters, which would explain why PaLM 62B beats larger models and why base GPT-3 175B gains little.

The chain-of-thought threshold was measured by final-answer match on multi-token answers, exactly the kind of metric the artefact account says manufactures thresholds. Wei et al. note small models often produce no parseable answer. Neither claim entails the other; the artefact account predicts the threshold should soften under a graded metric, which nobody in either subgraph has tested.

The chain-of-thought threshold is one claimed instance of a sharp emergent ability (Wei et al. call it 'an emergent ability of model scale'); evidence for it supports the general claim, not the reverse.
A threshold implies small-model results do not extrapolate, but the chain-of-thought claim does not assert unpredictability.
